findings.text: The first lines tell a newcomer what Athena is and give a reason to care: one model does the work, a different one checks it, and cost is recorded. This is clear, but it is the only text about Athena itself before the page switches to firstmate.
findings.source: Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost.

findings.text: This is the Athena site's address, but almost all of the page is a detailed study of a different project, firstmate. The opening explains that the study is meant as a demonstration, so a newcomer understands the purpose. Still, they must work through a lot of firstmate detail they did not come for.
findings.source: This page is that study of firstmate.

findings.text: A next step is offered at the very top and links to a Next steps section at the end. A newcomer always has a way out to the action.
findings.source: Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself

findings.text: The install step assumes the reader already has a checkout. It gives no clone command and no prerequisites, even though the page says Athena is written in Rust. The next line, `athena ask "add a changelog"`, does not say what the reader will see or where the change will go.
findings.source: Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh

findings.text: The claim-and-source system is explained up front, and every claim links to exact lines at a pinned commit. This shows Athena's value concretely, and a newcomer can check any statement.
findings.source: Each statement below ends with the id of the claim that supports it; the claims, with links to their sources, are listed at the end.

findings.text: The Start here section and its 'Words used first' list give a usable short tour of firstmate: what it is, one piece of work start to finish, and what happens on failure. A reader who stops here gets the gist.
The Counters section refers to transitions t1 to t11 before the Transitions section defines them. A newcomer reading top to bottom meets these ids with no meaning yet.
findings.source: places-held, changed by transitions t1, t3, t4, t9, t11

findings.text: This sentence is awkward and a little confusing, because the explanations come right after the paragraph, before the cards. The cards themselves are dense, with exit codes, locks and pending-close records, which is a lot for a first-time reader.
findings.source: The two deciders are explained below the cards' heading.

findings.text: The early definitions use terms that have not been explained yet, such as 'secondmate'. The glossary entry for ship ('A kind of task, named next to scouts') does not say what a ship is.
findings.source: home: A firstmate home is the place that holds a backlog of tasks. A secondmate is a persistent home of its own, not a task in someone else's backlog.

findings.text: The 'About this page' section and the footer describe internal repository layout. This means nothing to a newcomer and does not tell them what to do.
findings.source: This page's study id, firstmate-work-handling, is the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from.
